title: Project tutorial
summary: Get comfortable with the Unix file tree, a terminal, basic shell commands, SSH keys, and the Git workflow before starting the programming exercises.
why: A C source file lives in a directory, is edited and compiled through tools, and is submitted through Git. Knowing these tools makes the later programming tasks easier to start, test, and explain.
prerequisites: A terminal and a project repository

statedGoals.text: Introduce the basic skills and knowledge needed to start in good conditions.
Build programming foundations through reasoning, repetition, autonomy, and peer learning.
Identify and understand files, directories, tree structure, and the Unix root directory.
Discover terminal commands, command options, the current directory, file listings, hidden files, navigation, creation, permissions, editing, removal, and manual pages.
Research repositories and version control; understand why programmers save versions of their code.
Generate an SSH key pair, share the public key, keep the private key secret, then clone the project repository.
Practice untracked, staged, modified, committed, and pushed states and check that the remote copy contains the work.

interpretation: The tutorial builds the working environment around programming: locate the right file, change it deliberately, inspect the result, and save a reviewable history. The two exercises check exact file bytes and the ability to identify a public SSH key. The later C lessons rely on this workflow but do not require reproducing every tutorial command as a submission.

title: Shell fundamentals
summary: Create and inspect Unix files, directories, permissions, timestamps, links, listings, archives, and names containing special shell characters.
why: Commands act on files and metadata, not just the text inside them. Correct paths, quoting, permissions, and submitted archives are essential when compiling and submitting C projects.

statedGoals.text: Learn shell scripting basics, file manipulation, and Unix permission handling.
Build foundations through reasoning, peer learning, and developing the ability to find solutions.

interpretation: The exercises turn a long file listing into a specification. They ask you to control individual metadata fields and understand why the shell treats some filename characters as syntax unless they are quoted or escaped. Hard links and symbolic links are inferred learning targets from the requested link counts and listing.

exercises.title: testShell00
requirements: Directory: ex0/; submit testShell00.tar.
Create testShell00 with listing attributes -r--r-xr-x, one link, 40-byte size, and modification date Jun 1 23:42.
The total line and fields marked XX are not required to match.
Create the archive with tar -cf testShell00.tar testShell00.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Read a long listing as separate facts and change each required fact deliberately. File contents, permissions, and timestamps are different parts of file state.
exercises.connection: The tutorial introduced editing, listings, and access rights. This task requires exact control of those attributes and packaging the result.
exercises.observe: Highlight only the metadata changed by each command: writing affects bytes, chmod affects access rights, touch can affect time, and tar creates a separate archive.

exercises.title: Oh yeah, mooore...
requirements: Directory: ex1/; submit ex1.tar.
Create the listed directories and files test0 through test6 so ls -l matches all specified fields; XX fields may differ.
test0: directory, rwx--xr-x, link count 2, Jun 1 20:47. test1: regular file, rwx--xr--, link count 1, 4 bytes, Jun 1 21:46.
test2: directory, r-x---r--, link count 2, Jun 1 22:45. test3: regular file, r-----r--, link count 2, 1 byte, Jun 1 23:44.
test4: regular file, rw-r----x, link count 1, 2 bytes, Jun 1 23:43. test5: regular file, r-----r--, link count 2, 1 byte, Jun 1 23:44.
test6: symbolic link to test0, lrwxrwxrwx, link count 1, displayed size 5, Jun 1 22:20.
Create the submission archive with tar -cf ex1.tar * after the requested entries exist.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Learn that names and stored file data are separate. A hard link gives the same underlying file another name; a symbolic link stores a path to follow. Directory permissions control different actions from file permissions.
exercises.connection: The first exercise controlled a single file. This one adds several entry types, relationships, and independent metadata values.
exercises.observe: Show two hard-linked names sharing one inode and contents, while a symbolic link has its own inode and target text. Highlight shared changes and separately show directory traversal permission.

exercises.title: midLS
requirements: Directory: ex2/; submit midLS containing the requested command line.
List files and directories in the current directory, excluding hidden entries and all names beginning with a dot, including dot and dot-dot.
Separate names with a comma followed by a space, order them by modification date, and add a slash after directory names.
Do not add unrequested output.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Choose command options according to a required result, then inspect how filtering, ordering, and formatting affect the same set of directory entries.
exercises.connection: Earlier listings revealed metadata. Here modification time becomes the ordering key, and file type controls a visible suffix.
exercises.observe: The file tree stays unchanged. Watch dot-prefixed names disappear from the displayed list, dates determine order, and directory names receive slashes.

exercises.title: Can you create it ?
requirements: Directory: ex3/; submit the file whose exact name is shown in the subject: "\?$*'MaRViN'*$?\".
The file must contain exactly the two bytes 42, with no newline or other content.
The example listing also shows -rw---xr-- permissions and a 2-byte size; inspect the example details.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Separate literal characters from shell syntax. Quotes and backslashes can be data in a filename, while unprotected shell characters can change how a command is interpreted.
exercises.connection: Creating ordinary filenames was simple. This task requires the same file operation while controlling how the shell parses the name and the exact contents.
exercises.observe: Show the requested name as literal data, highlight which command characters protect it from interpretation, and show a two-byte file without a newline.

title: Git fundamentals
summary: Inspect the history of a Git repository and list existing ignored files through small shell scripts.
why: Git records versions of source files. History helps explain what was changed, and ignore rules keep generated binaries, object files, and unrelated local files out of the submitted project.
prerequisites: Repository, commit, staging, and shell scripts

statedGoals.text: Learn and practice fundamental Git commands and SSH key management through shell scripting.
Build foundations through reasoning and peer-learning exchange.

interpretation: The two numbered exercises focus on querying Git's state: recent commit identifiers and files matched by ignore rules. SSH key management is part of the stated module summary, but it is not a separate numbered exercise here; it was directly practiced in the project tutorial.

exercises.title: GiT commit
requirements: Directory: ex0/; submit git_commit.sh.
Create a shell script that displays the identifiers of the last five commits in the Git repository.
The sample output shows a full commit identifier on each line, with no other commit information.
The evaluator will run the script in its own environment; do not hard-code the example identifiers.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Ask Git for repository history and select the fields and number of entries the task requests. Commit identifiers come from the repository being inspected.
exercises.connection: The tutorial created commits and used a history command. This task narrows that history to exact, script-friendly output.
exercises.observe: Show a fictional commit chain with HEAD at its latest commit. Select the five newest identifiers in history order; the query changes output but creates no commit.

exercises.title: gitignore
requirements: Directory: ex1/; submit git_ignore.sh.
Write a short shell script that lists all existing files ignored by the Git repository.
The evaluator will use its own environment; query actual ignored files rather than copying the sample names.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Understand that an ignore pattern is a rule while an ignored file is an existing entry matched by a rule. Already tracked files do not become untracked merely because an ignore rule is added.
exercises.connection: The tutorial showed untracked, staged, and committed files. Ignore handling adds another distinction useful for keeping compiler outputs out of commits.
exercises.observe: Show the file tree beside ignore patterns and Git status. A rule matches existing untracked examples; listing ignored files leaves them on disk.

sourceNotes: Exercise 0 is GiT commit in the chapter title and GiT commit? in the assignment table; exercise 1 is gitignore in the heading but GiT in the table. Records use the chapter headings.

title: Shell searching and finding
summary: Search a directory tree, select entries by name or type, transform output, remove selected files, and count files and directories.
why: As projects grow, a command must reliably inspect many nested entries. Search predicates, exact output, and deliberate deletion are useful for locating source files and managing build artifacts.

statedGoals.text: Learn to search, filter, and manipulate files using shell scripting and Unix command-line utilities.
Build foundations through reasoning, verification, and peer-learning exchange.

interpretation: These exercises combine recursive traversal with selection rules and an action. The learning progression is to display selected names, then act on selected files, then count selected entry types. Exact matching and traversal scope matter as much as choosing a command.

exercises.title: find_sh
requirements: Directory: ex0/; submit find_sh.sh.
Write a command line searching the current directory and every subdirectory for filenames ending in .sh.
Display only the filenames, without the .sh extension; do not retain directory paths.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Turn a nested directory tree into a list, select names by a pattern, and transform each matching path into the output the task asks for.
exercises.connection: The file-tree tutorial explains why searching the current directory is different from searching every descendant. Shell quoting prevents the current shell from expanding the pattern too early.
exercises.observe: Highlight each visited entry, whether its filename matches, and how a matching path becomes a basename with its final .sh removed. No files change.

exercises.title: clean
requirements: Directory: ex1/; submit clean containing the command line.
Search the current directory and all subdirectories for files ending in ~, or whose name both starts and ends with #.
Display and delete every found file.
Use only one command; no semicolon, &&, or other command-chaining tricks.
The subject directs students to man find.
Authorized field: None.
exercises.goal: Express two selection rules in one search and apply an action only to matches. Understand which names qualify before any deletion happens.
exercises.connection: find_sh only displayed matches. clean uses the same traversal idea but adds a state-changing action and combines two name patterns.
exercises.observe: Use a virtual file tree. Highlight matches, show their names in output, and remove only those matched entries from the after-state. Include near-misses such as #draft and draft#.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Select, display, and remove backup files

exercises.title: count_files
requirements: Directory: ex2/; submit count_files.sh.
Write a command line counting and displaying all regular files and directories in the current directory and every subdirectory.
Include the starting directory . in the count.
The sample 42 is illustrative; derive the count from the actual tree.
Authorized field: None.
concepts: Including the root of a search
exercises.goal: Count entries by their types and scope. The starting directory is one of the directories being counted, not just a place to begin.
exercises.connection: Earlier exercises selected entries by their names. Here selection uses file type, then combines the selected entries into one number.
exercises.observe: Increment a visible count for each regular file or directory, including .; show excluded entry types separately. Output is one final number and the tree remains unchanged.

sourceNotes: The assignment tables say find_sh.sh and count_files.sh, while their chapter headings are find_sh and count_files. Records use chapter headings and preserve required submission filenames separately.

title: C Programming Fundamentals
summary: Make small C functions that display characters, walk through letters and digits, and choose output based on a number's sign.
why: These exercises make the execution of a program visible. You learn that computing a value and displaying that value are separate actions, and that a loop needs a starting value, a condition, and a change that eventually stops it.
prerequisites: Create and edit a text file
Navigate a directory in the shell
Compile a C source file with cc

statedGoals.text: Implement fundamental C functions to display characters, the alphabet, numbers, and check integer signs using standard output.
Understand how computers store and manipulate data before writing the first C program.
Practice loops and conditional branches, both separately and together.
Develop programming foundations through practice, experimentation, and discussion with peers.

interpretation: The exercise sequence appears designed to build a mental model of declarations, assignments, character values, function parameters, loops, and if/else decisions. A beginner should be able to predict the next value and the next visible character before advancing. The tutorial also introduces an empty main, compilation, invisible calculation, ASCII values, and changing a loop counter; these are useful introductory simulations even though they are not numbered exercises.

exercises.title: ft_putchar
requirements: Submit ex0/ft_putchar.c.
Prototype: void ft_putchar(char c);
Display the character supplied as the parameter.
Authorized function: write.
The subject explicitly specifies write(1, &c, 1) to display the character.
Submit the requested function, without a main; a separate main can be used as a learning/test harness.
The module requires cc with -Wall -Wextra -Werror and the 42 Norm.
exercises.goal: Understand how a character travels from a call into a function and then becomes visible terminal output.
exercises.connection: A shell command runs the compiled program. Inside that program, main can call a smaller function with a character as its argument.
exercises.observe: The parameter c receives its own character value. &c identifies where that value is stored. write receives that address and reads one byte for output; it does not change c. The first 1 selects standard output, and the last 1 is the byte count.

exercises.title: ft_print_alphabet
requirements: Submit ex1/ft_print_alphabet.c.
Prototype: void ft_print_alphabet(void);
Display the lowercase alphabet on one line in ascending order, starting at 'a'.
Authorized function: write.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Learn to repeat a small action while moving through an ordered range.
exercises.connection: Repeat the one-character output operation from ft_putchar. A changing variable selects a different character each time.
exercises.observe: The condition is checked before each iteration. Printing changes terminal output while leaving the character unchanged; incrementing changes the character while leaving existing output unchanged. On an ASCII-based learning example, 'a' + 1 gives 'b'. After 'z', the condition becomes false.

exercises.title: ft_print_reverse_alphabet
requirements: Submit ex2/ft_print_reverse_alphabet.c.
Prototype: void ft_print_reverse_alphabet(void);
Display the lowercase alphabet on one line in descending order, starting at 'z'.
Authorized function: write.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Learn how the starting point, condition, and direction of change work together in a loop.
exercises.connection: Use the same loop structure as the forward alphabet, but start at the other end and move downward.
exercises.observe: Compare the variable before and after a decrement, and follow the accumulated output. The stopping comparison must match a descending loop. The final valid character is printed before the next condition becomes false.

exercises.title: ft_print_numbers
requirements: Submit ex3/ft_print_numbers.c.
Prototype: void ft_print_numbers(void);
Display all digits on one line in ascending order.
Authorized function: write.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Distinguish a numerical value from the character used to display that number.
exercises.connection: The alphabet loop also applies to the ordered digit characters '0' through '9'.
exercises.observe: In an ASCII example, the character '0' has code 48, which differs from the integer 0. Adding an integer digit to '0' produces the printable digit character. write prints bytes, so writing the raw low byte of integer 5 would not print the character '5'.

exercises.title: ft_is_negative
requirements: Submit ex4/ft_is_negative.c.
Prototype: void ft_is_negative(int n);
Display 'N' when n is negative; display 'P' when n is positive or zero.
Authorized function: write.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Learn how a comparison selects exactly one path through the program.
exercises.connection: Earlier examples repeat output through loops. This example chooses one output using a condition.
exercises.observe: Show the copied parameter n, the truth value of n < 0, the selected line, and the skipped branch. Demonstrate a negative number, zero, and a positive number; zero belongs to the 'P' branch.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Choose a branch from a number's sign

title: C Character Arithmetic
summary: Convert numbers into printable characters and use ordered loops to generate combinations without duplicates.
why: C does not automatically turn an integer into a sequence of display characters when write is used. Division and remainder help extract digits; well-chosen loop bounds help generate exactly the combinations requested.

statedGoals.text: Focus on number manipulation and arithmetic operations in C.

interpretation: These exercises appear to develop decimal decomposition, the difference between digits and digit characters, nested loops, ordering constraints, and exact output formatting. ft_putnbr also requires careful thinking about the smallest representable int because its positive counterpart might not fit in the same int type. Generating combinations teaches how to avoid duplicates through the construction of candidates instead of filtering every possible candidate afterwards.

exercises.title: ft_putnbr
requirements: Submit ex0/ft_putnbr.c.
Prototype: void ft_putnbr(int nb);
Display the integer passed as a parameter.
Support every value representable by int, including zero and the minimum int value.
Authorized function: write.
The subject's example displays 42 for ft_putnbr(42).
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Understand how a multi-digit number becomes several character writes in the correct order.
exercises.connection: Build on printing one digit. Division by 10 separates earlier digits, remainder by 10 finds the last digit, and adding '0' makes a printable character.
exercises.observe: Use a small input such as 426 to show division and remainder. Show why discovering the final digit first does not mean printing it first. Trace zero separately and explain that negating the minimum int directly can overflow; the teaching example must use a safe approach. If recursion is chosen, distinguish each call's own nb and the output produced as calls return.

exercises.title: ft_print_comb
requirements: Submit ex1/ft_print_comb.c.
Prototype: void ft_print_comb(void);
Display all combinations of three different digits, with digits ascending within each combination and combinations listed in ascending order.
The illustrated output starts 012, 013, 014 and ends 789, with comma-space separators.
Do not include an alternate ordering such as 987 when 789 is already included, or repeated digits such as 999.
Authorized function: write.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Learn to use relationships between loop variables to generate unique ordered combinations.
exercises.connection: Expand a one-variable character loop into three related loops. Conditions decide when a comma-space separator is needed.
exercises.observe: Show the three counters together. When the innermost loop ends, its outer counter advances and it is reinitialized from that counter. a < b < c automatically prevents repeated digits and alternate orders. At 789, output formatting changes so no further separator is written.

exercises.title: ft_print_comb2
requirements: Submit ex2/ft_print_comb2.c.
Prototype: void ft_print_comb2(void);
Display every different combination of two two-digit numbers between 00 and 99 in ascending order.
The illustrated output starts 00 01, 00 02 and ends 97 99, 98 99, using a space within each pair and comma-space separators between pairs.
Represent each number with two digits, including a leading zero where needed.
The illustrated ascending pairs use a smaller first number than second number.
Authorized function: write.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Combine ordered pair generation with converting each number into its tens and units characters.
exercises.connection: Use the distinct ordered-counter idea from ft_print_comb and the digit extraction idea from ft_putnbr.
exercises.observe: Track a and b independently from the four output characters. For value 7, integer division by 10 gives 0 and remainder gives 7, producing '0' and '7'. The second loop restarts at a + 1. At pair 98 99, skip the following separator.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Generate ordered pairs with two-digit formatting

title: C Algorithmic Fundamentals
summary: Solve small mathematical problems using loops and recursive calls, then follow how computed results return to the caller.
why: Comparing iterative and recursive versions helps separate a problem's rule from the method used to execute it. Tracing parameters, local variables, waiting calls, and return values prepares you for strings, linked structures, trees, and backtracking.

statedGoals.text: Introduce fundamental algorithmic concepts in C, focusing on recursion, mathematical computations, and problem-solving techniques.
Understand the execution timeline in which a caller waits while a called function runs and continues after the called function returns.
Understand that recursive calls have distinct parameters and ordinary local variables.
Calculate a total through the return values of recursive calls rather than returning a fixed number.

interpretation: The paired factorial and power exercises appear designed to compare a loop's changing accumulator with a recursive chain of waiting calls. Fibonacci introduces a function that makes two smaller recursive calls. The tutorial stresses stopping recursion and finite memory. Its static count variable is shared by calls, unlike ordinary automatic local variables; a simulator should make that distinction explicit if it discusses the tutorial's counter. Use small values with defined arithmetic; these exercises explicitly do not ask students to handle integer overflow.

exercises.title: ft_iterative_factorial
requirements: Submit ex0/ft_iterative_factorial.c.
Prototype: int ft_iterative_factorial(int nb);
Use an iterative function to return the factorial of the supplied number.
Return 0 for an invalid argument; the exercise does not define the word 'invalid' further.
Overflow must not be handled; the subject says the resulting function return is undefined.
Authorized functions: none.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Learn to build a result by repeatedly updating one accumulator and then return it.
exercises.connection: The earlier loops printed a character on each iteration. This loop changes a numerical result instead, and returns that result to its caller.
exercises.observe: Trace a small factorial such as 4! through an accumulator and counter. Show multiplication before and after every iteration, why the initial product is 1, and how returning a result differs from printing. Mathematical factorial supplies 0! = 1 and negative inputs as invalid; label these explanations as interpretation of the mathematical operation.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Build a factorial with an accumulator

exercises.title: ft_recursive_factorial
requirements: Submit ex1/ft_recursive_factorial.c.
Prototype: int ft_recursive_factorial(int nb);
Use recursion to return the factorial of the supplied number.
Return 0 for an invalid argument; the exercise does not define the word 'invalid' further.
Overflow must not be handled; the subject says the resulting function return is undefined.
Authorized functions: none; the required recursive call to the function itself is part of the exercise.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Understand that each recursive call works on a smaller input while its caller waits for a result.
exercises.connection: Use the same factorial rule as the iterative exercise. Instead of updating one accumulator, keep separate calls whose unfinished multiplication resumes after the smaller call returns.
exercises.observe: For 4!, show distinct nb values in each call. The caller retains its own nb when it passes nb - 1. A base case returns 1; the result then travels back through waiting multiplications. Avoid depicting all calls as sharing a single nb variable.

exercises.title: ft_iterative_power
requirements: Submit ex2/ft_iterative_power.c.
Prototype: int ft_iterative_power(int nb, int power);
Use iteration to return nb raised to power.
A negative power returns 0.
Overflow must not be handled.
The subject explicitly defines 0 to power 0 as returning 1.
Authorized functions: none.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Learn how a loop count and a multiplication value play different roles in a calculation.
exercises.connection: Like iterative factorial, an accumulator starts at 1. Here the multiplier stays fixed while the number of multiplications depends on power.
exercises.observe: Trace 2 raised to 3 as successive results 1, 2, 4, 8. Show which value stays constant and which value controls termination. With exponent zero, no multiplication is needed and the initial result 1 is returned. A negative exponent takes the early return path.

exercises.title: ft_recursive_power
requirements: Submit ex3/ft_recursive_power.c.
Prototype: int ft_recursive_power(int nb, int power);
Use recursion to return nb raised to power.
A negative power returns 0.
Overflow must not be handled; the subject says the resulting function return is undefined.
The subject explicitly defines 0 to power 0 as returning 1.
Authorized functions: none; the required recursive call to the function itself is part of the exercise.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Follow a recursive problem in which one parameter stays the same while the other moves toward a stopping case.
exercises.connection: Compare recursive factorial and iterative power. Each call copies the base and a smaller exponent, then waits to multiply its returned result by the base.
exercises.observe: Trace 2 raised to 3. Show separate call frames with exponents 3, 2, 1, 0 and the same base 2. The zero-exponent call returns 1. Show each waiting multiplication resume in order; include the explicit 0^0 rule and negative-exponent early return.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: A fixed base through recursive calls

exercises.title: ft_fibonacci
requirements: Submit ex4/ft_fibonacci.c.
Prototype: int ft_fibonacci(int index);
Return the element at the supplied zero-based index in the Fibonacci sequence, beginning 0, 1, 1, 2.
The function must be recursive.
A negative index returns -1.
Overflow must not be handled; the subject says the resulting function return is undefined.
Authorized functions: none; the required recursive calls to the function itself are part of the exercise.
Submit the function; main is not requested.
exercises.goal: Understand how a recursive result can depend on two smaller results, and why two base cases are needed.
exercises.connection: Factorial and power each need one smaller recursive result. Fibonacci needs two; the index is a position rather than the value at that position.
exercises.observe: Use a small index such as 4. Show index 0 returning 0 and index 1 returning 1, then show results being added. Multiple calls can calculate the same index but still have separate call frames. Do not claim that C guarantees left-to-right evaluation of the two operands in fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); the teaching example can assign each result in a separate statement to make the displayed order explicit.

title: C Pointers
summary: A pointer stores an address. Follow that address to read or change an existing value, then use this idea to exchange numbers and rearrange arrays.
why: Pointers let a function work on the caller's variables and let one parameter describe an entire array. They prepare you for strings, allocated memory, and linked structures.

statedGoals.text: Practice pointer assignment, swapping, arithmetic operations, and array manipulation.
Use address-of and dereferencing to print and update the same integer through its name and a pointer.
Explore moving through a string with pointer arithmetic and modifying an integer through a pointer parameter.

interpretation: The exercises gradually separate a stored address from the value at that address: one level of indirection, nine levels, two independent targets, multiple outputs, then array transformations. A copied pointer parameter can still refer to the caller's memory.

exercises.title: ft_ft
requirements: Submit ft_ft.c in ex0/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_ft(int *nbr);
Set the integer pointed to by nbr to 42.
exercises.goal: Understand that writing through a pointer changes the original integer rather than an independent copy.
exercises.connection: A normal int parameter receives a copy of a number. Here the function receives a copy of an address and follows it to the caller's integer.
exercises.observe: Show the caller's integer, its address, and the function's pointer parameter. After *nbr = 42, only the pointed integer changes; the pointer keeps the same address.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Set a caller's integer through a pointer

exercises.title: ft_ultimate_ft
requirements: Submit ft_ultimate_ft.c in ex1/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_ultimate_ft(int *********nbr);
Follow nine pointer levels and set the final integer to 42.
exercises.goal: Trace a chain of addresses without confusing an intermediate pointer with the final integer.
exercises.connection: Every * repeats the single dereference learned in ft_ft. Intermediate results are still addresses until all nine levels have been followed.
exercises.observe: Show nine address links ending in one int. Expand the chain one link at a time, then highlight only the final int changing to 42.

exercises.title: ft_swap
requirements: Submit ft_swap.c in ex2/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_swap(int *a, int *b);
Exchange the values of the two integers whose addresses are passed.
exercises.goal: Preserve one old value before overwriting it so both caller variables receive the correct value.
exercises.connection: ft_ft changes one caller value. Swapping combines two such writes with a local value copy.
exercises.observe: For 3 and 8, show tmp = 3, then the first value becoming 8, then the second becoming 3. Pointer addresses stay fixed.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Swap two integers with a temporary

exercises.title: ft_div_mod
requirements: Submit ft_div_mod.c in ex3/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_div_mod(int a, int b, int *div, int *mod);
Store a / b in the integer pointed to by div and a % b in the integer pointed to by mod.
exercises.goal: Use pointer parameters to return two results from a void function.
exercises.connection: Combine arithmetic from earlier modules with writing to caller variables through pointers.
exercises.observe: Use 17 and 5. Separate copied inputs from output addresses. Highlight div changing to 3 and mod changing to 2 while original inputs remain 17 and 5.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Send quotient and remainder to output variables

exercises.title: ft_ultimate_div_mod
requirements: Submit ft_ultimate_div_mod.c in ex4/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_ultimate_div_mod(int *a, int *b);
Replace *a with the quotient of the original integers and *b with their remainder.
exercises.goal: Calculate both answers from the original inputs before overwriting values needed by later calculations.
exercises.connection: ft_div_mod had separate input and output storage. Here the same two locations are both inputs and outputs, so write order matters.
exercises.observe: Show 17 and 5 before the call, keep one computed result temporarily, and finish with 3 and 2. Explain why calculating the remainder after replacing 17 with 3 would be wrong.

exercises.title: ft_rev_int_tab
requirements: Submit ft_rev_int_tab.c in ex5/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_rev_int_tab(int *tab, int size);
Reverse the array in place; the first element becomes last.
Parameters are the first integer's pointer and the number of integers.
exercises.goal: Move inward from both ends and reverse an array without losing values or swapping the same pair twice.
exercises.connection: Reuse ft_swap's temporary-value pattern on elements accessed through the array's first address.
exercises.observe: Highlight the two chosen cells, the temporary, both writes, and indices moving inward. An odd-length middle element should remain untouched.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Reverse an array from both ends

exercises.title: ft_sort_int_tab
requirements: Submit ft_sort_int_tab.c in ex6/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: void ft_sort_int_tab(int *tab, int size);
Sort the integer array into ascending order.
Parameters are the first integer's pointer and the number of integers.
exercises.goal: Arrange values by repeatedly comparing positions and correcting their order.
exercises.connection: Combine pointer-based array access, conditions, loops, and the swap operation.
exercises.observe: Show comparison steps separately from actual swaps. Track which part is sorted, and include equal values and negative values in a small example.

title: C Simple Strings
summary: Treat a string as characters followed by a zero byte. Read each character, decide whether it belongs to a category, transform letters, count characters, and print them.
why: String processing turns raw memory into useful text. Correctly recognizing the end of a string prevents reading or writing beyond its characters.

statedGoals.text: Implement basic string functions for alphabetic and numeric checks, case changes, and length calculations.

interpretation: These exercises practice scanning a zero-terminated sequence, reporting a property without modifying it, modifying writable characters in place, and sending bytes to standard output. Empty strings and word boundaries make the loop rules precise.

exercises.title: ft_str_is_alpha
requirements: Submit ft_str_is_alpha.c in ex0/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_str_is_alpha(char *str);
Return 1 for a string containing only alphabetical characters; return 0 if any other character occurs.
Return 1 for an empty string.
exercises.goal: Check every character and stop at the first one that violates the rule.
exercises.connection: Pointer arithmetic from the previous lesson advances through characters; conditions classify each byte.
exercises.observe: Highlight one character at a time, show its code and the two letter-range tests, and show the return value becoming 0 on a digit or punctuation.

exercises.title: ft_str_is_numeric
requirements: Submit ft_str_is_numeric.c in ex1/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_str_is_numeric(char *str);
Return 1 only when all characters are digits, otherwise 0.
Return 1 for an empty string.
exercises.goal: Distinguish a text digit such as '7' from the numeric integer 7 and recognize only digit characters.
exercises.connection: Reuse alphabetic validation's traversal but change the accepted character range.
exercises.observe: Show '0' through '9' passing, a sign or space failing, and the zero terminator ending the loop without being tested as a digit.

exercises.title: ft_str_is_lowercase
requirements: Submit ft_str_is_lowercase.c in ex2/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_str_is_lowercase(char *str);
Return 1 only for lowercase alphabetical characters, otherwise 0.
Return 1 for an empty string.
exercises.goal: Apply a more specific character rule while leaving the original string unchanged.
exercises.connection: Narrow the alphabetical test to lowercase letters.
exercises.observe: Show lowercase letters passing and an uppercase letter or digit causing an early 0 return.

exercises.title: ft_str_is_uppercase
requirements: Submit ft_str_is_uppercase.c in ex3/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_str_is_uppercase(char *str);
Return 1 only for uppercase alphabetical characters, otherwise 0.
Return 1 for an empty string.
exercises.goal: Check a string property without accidentally modifying the inspected characters.
exercises.connection: Mirror the lowercase predicate with the uppercase range.
exercises.observe: Show 'A' and 'Z' passing, lowercase letters failing, and no memory contents changing during validation.

exercises.title: ft_str_is_printable
requirements: Submit ft_str_is_printable.c in ex4/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_str_is_printable(char *str);
Return 1 only when all characters are printable, otherwise 0.
Return 1 for an empty string.
exercises.goal: Recognize that a stored character can be a control byte rather than a visible letter or symbol.
exercises.connection: Extend character-range validation beyond letters and digits.
exercises.observe: Display a newline as an escaped byte, distinguish space from newline, and explain why control characters fail a printable-ASCII example.

exercises.title: ft_strupcase
requirements: Submit ft_strupcase.c in ex5/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strupcase(char *str);
Transform letters to uppercase and return str.
exercises.goal: Modify selected characters through the string's address and return the original starting address.
exercises.connection: Combine validation's letter test with pointer-based assignment.
exercises.observe: Use a writable array, highlight each lowercase byte before and after conversion, and show digits and punctuation unchanged. The returned pointer must still identify the first character.

exercises.title: ft_strlowcase
requirements: Submit ft_strlowcase.c in ex6/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strlowcase(char *str);
Transform letters to lowercase and return str.
exercises.goal: Use a condition to write only the uppercase letters that need conversion.
exercises.connection: Reverse the uppercase conversion while keeping the same traversal and pointer identity.
exercises.observe: Show uppercase bytes becoming lowercase and all other bytes staying the same, including the zero terminator.

exercises.title: ft_strcapitalize
requirements: Submit ft_strcapitalize.c in ex7/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strcapitalize(char *str);
Capitalize the first letter of each word and lowercase the remaining letters.
A word is a sequence of alphanumeric characters.
Return str.
The example leaves 42words beginning with a digit and capitalizes words separated by hyphens, plus signs, or punctuation.
exercises.goal: Remember whether the next alphanumeric character begins a word and apply the correct letter transformation.
exercises.connection: Build a small state machine from alphabetic/numeric tests and case conversion.
exercises.observe: Show a new-word flag changing at separators. Use '42WORDS hi+THERE' so the digit starts the first word and W becomes lowercase rather than uppercase.

exercises.title: ft_strlen
requirements: Submit ft_strlen.c in ex8/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_strlen(char *str);
Count and return the number of characters in a string.
exercises.goal: Count characters before the terminator without counting the terminator itself.
exercises.connection: Reuse the character traversal without any validation or memory writes.
exercises.observe: For 'cat', show four stored bytes but a length of three, and show an empty string returning zero.

exercises.title: ft_putstr
requirements: Submit ft_putstr.c in ex9/.
Authorized functions: write.
Prototype: void ft_putstr(char *str);
Display the string on standard output.
exercises.goal: Send characters to the terminal while leaving the string's stored bytes unchanged.
exercises.connection: Combine string traversal with the write-based output used in earlier character exercises.
exercises.observe: Highlight the source byte passed to write and append the character to terminal output. Explain that '\0' stops traversal and is not printed.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Print a string one byte at a time

exercises.title: ft_putstr_non_printable
requirements: Submit ft_putstr_non_printable.c in ex10/.
Authorized functions: write.
Prototype: void ft_putstr_non_printable(char *str);
Print printable characters normally.
Print nonprintable characters as lowercase hexadecimal preceded by a backslash; the example turns newline into \0a.
exercises.goal: Represent invisible bytes as readable text without changing the original string.
exercises.connection: Combine printable-character tests, arithmetic quotient/remainder, and terminal output.
exercises.observe: Show a newline's value 10, hexadecimal digits 0 and a, and the three emitted characters '\', '0', 'a'. Treat high bytes as unsigned values in the teaching example.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Render a control byte in hexadecimal

title: C Memory Management
summary: Request storage at runtime, fill it, and return its address. Allocate arrays and strings, expose a new pointer through a pointer-to-pointer, and build collections of strings.
why: A function often cannot know the required size until it sees its inputs. Dynamic allocation lets results outlive the function, but the caller must understand ownership and eventual cleanup.

statedGoals.text: Implement dynamic memory management functions, including allocation, string operations, and base conversion.

interpretation: The sequence develops allocation sizing, independent copies, half-open ranges, output pointer ownership, combined result buffers, and nested allocations. Knowing how much memory exists and who must release it is the central skill.

exercises.title: ft_strdup
requirements: Submit ft_strdup.c in ex0/.
Authorized functions: malloc.
Prototype: char *ft_strdup(char *src);
Reproduce strdup behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Allocate a separate writable string rather than merely copying the source address.
exercises.connection: String counting determines the needed storage and character copying fills it; pointers identify the new buffer.
exercises.observe: Show source and destination at different addresses, allocate strlen(src)+1 bytes, copy each character and '\0', and show changing the clone does not change the source.

exercises.title: ft_range
requirements: Submit ft_range.c in ex1/.
Authorized functions: malloc.
Prototype: int *ft_range(int min, int max);
Return an allocated integer array covering min inclusive to max exclusive.
Return a null pointer when min is greater than or equal to max.
exercises.goal: Calculate a required count from inputs and allocate enough bytes for that many integers.
exercises.connection: Array access and pointer arithmetic remain the same; the array's storage now comes from an allocation.
exercises.observe: For min=2 and max=5, show a count of 3, storage for three ints, then values 2, 3, 4. Separately show the invalid-range path returning NULL.

exercises.title: ft_ultimate_range
requirements: Submit ft_ultimate_range.c in ex2/.
Authorized functions: malloc.
Prototype: int ft_ultimate_range(int **range, int min, int max);
Allocate and assign an array for min inclusive to max exclusive.
Return its element count, or -1 on error.
When min is greater than or equal to max, set the caller's range pointer to NULL and return 0.
exercises.goal: Change a caller's pointer through its address while returning an independent count or error status.
exercises.connection: ft_div_mod wrote to caller integers; this exercise writes an allocated address to a caller pointer.
exercises.observe: Show range pointing to the caller's int* variable. After allocation, *range stores the heap address; the function return carries only the count. Keep allocation failure and an empty range visibly distinct.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Return an allocated array through int **

exercises.title: ft_strjoin
requirements: Submit ft_strjoin.c in ex3/.
Authorized functions: malloc.
Prototype: char *ft_strjoin(int size, char **strs, char *sep);
Concatenate size strings, placing sep between successive strings.
When size is 0, return an empty string that can be freed.
exercises.goal: Plan one result buffer large enough for several input strings and separators.
exercises.connection: Combine string lengths, string copies, and the pointer arrays needed for multiple text values.
exercises.observe: For ['red','blue'] and '/', show 3+1+4+1 bytes, source pointers staying fixed, destination filling with 'red/blue\0', and no trailing separator. A size-zero result still has one allocated zero byte.

exercises.title: ft_convert_base
requirements: Submit ft_convert_base.c and ft_convert_base2.c in ex4/.
Authorized functions: malloc, free.
Prototype: char *ft_convert_base(char *nbr, char *base_from, char *base_to);
Convert the numeric string from the source symbol alphabet to the destination symbol alphabet.
nbr and both base strings may be non-writable; do not modify them.
The represented number must fit in an int.
Return NULL for an invalid base: empty or one-character base, duplicate symbols, or '+', '-', or whitespace in the symbols.
Prefix the result only with a single '-' when needed, with no whitespace or '+'.
The prototype continues on PDF page 15.
exercises.goal: Separate a number's value from the symbols used to write it and construct a new representation without altering the inputs.
exercises.connection: Build on digit parsing and quotient/remainder arithmetic, then apply dynamic allocation to the resulting string.
exercises.observe: Convert binary '101' to decimal '5': show accumulated values 1, 2, 5 and output digits. Include invalid duplicate-symbol and one-symbol bases. Show the sign separate from magnitude.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Convert a number between symbol alphabets

exercises.title: ft_split
requirements: Submit ft_split.c in ex5/.
Authorized functions: malloc.
Prototype: char **ft_split(char *str, char *charset);
Treat each character in charset as a separator.
Return an array of addresses of the substrings between separators.
The final pointer-array element must be 0.
Do not include empty strings in the result.
The input string may not be modified.
exercises.goal: Build an array of independently stored words while skipping runs of separators.
exercises.connection: Use string traversal to find word ranges, allocation to copy them, and pointer-to-pointer indexing to collect their addresses.
exercises.observe: For ',red,,blue;' and ',;', show skipped separators, two allocated words with their own zero bytes, and a three-slot pointer array ending in NULL. Distinguish the pointer-array terminator from each string's byte terminator.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Split text into an allocated string array

title: C Strings
summary: Copy, compare, append, and search strings by inspecting or transferring their bytes. Parse numeric text using whitespace, sign, and digit rules.
why: These operations are the building blocks of text processing. They make buffer capacity, string termination, byte comparison, and parser stopping conditions concrete.

statedGoals.text: Implement fundamental string functions, including validation, transformation, and concatenation operations.

interpretation: The actual exercises focus on copying, bounded copying, comparison, bounded comparison, appending, searching, and integer parsing. The module summary is broader than this exercise list. Learn each operation's distinct return and termination contract rather than treating every string loop as identical.

exercises.title: ft_strcpy
requirements: Submit ft_strcpy.c in ex0/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strcpy(char *dest, char *src);
Reproduce strcpy behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Transfer a complete string into existing writable storage while preserving the source.
exercises.connection: Use the same traversal as strlen, now writing each inspected character to another array.
exercises.observe: Show distinct source and destination addresses, each copied byte, the final copied '\0', and the returned starting destination address. Make destination capacity visible.

exercises.title: ft_strncpy
requirements: Submit ft_strncpy.c in ex1/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strncpy(char *dest, char *src, unsigned int n);
Reproduce strncpy behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Understand that an exact byte limit changes the termination behavior compared with strcpy.
exercises.connection: Add a count limit to copying and distinguish storage padding from a complete copied string.
exercises.observe: Show a short source zero-padded up to n and a long source copied for n bytes without an added terminator. Do not print the latter as a C string; inspect the bytes directly.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Compare padded and truncated bounded copies

exercises.title: ft_strcmp
requirements: Submit ft_strcmp.c in ex2/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_strcmp(char *s1, char *s2);
Reproduce strcmp behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Determine order using the first differing byte rather than string length or a comparison of addresses.
exercises.connection: Scan two strings together using the character codes already used for classification.
exercises.observe: For 'cat' and 'car', show c=c, a=a, then t versus r determining a positive result. Include an equal-string case and a prefix ending in '\0'.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Compare strings at the first differing byte

exercises.title: ft_strncmp
requirements: Submit ft_strncmp.c in ex3/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_strncmp(char *s1, char *s2, unsigned int n);
Reproduce strncmp behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Compare only the allowed prefix and stop safely at the limit or a terminator.
exercises.connection: Add a bound to strcmp, similar to adding a bound to copying but without padding or writes.
exercises.observe: Show 'cat' and 'car' comparing equal for n=2 but differing for n=3. A zero limit should return zero without reading character cells.

exercises.title: ft_strcat
requirements: Submit ft_strcat.c in ex4/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strcat(char *dest, char *src);
Reproduce strcat behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Append after an existing string instead of overwriting its beginning.
exercises.connection: First locate the terminator with a strlen-like scan, then copy using a strcpy-like scan.
exercises.observe: For 'hi' plus '!', highlight finding the old terminator, replacing it with '!', adding a new terminator, and leaving the returned pointer at the original start.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Append a string at the old terminator

exercises.title: ft_strncat
requirements: Submit ft_strncat.c in ex5/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strncat(char *dest, char *src, unsigned int nb);
Reproduce strncat behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Separate a limit on characters appended from the destination's total buffer capacity.
exercises.connection: Combine strcat's append position with a bounded source traversal.
exercises.observe: For 'hi' plus 'there' with nb=2, show 'hith\0'. Explain the limit controls appended characters and the destination still needs room for the old text plus those characters and a final zero byte.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Append a limited number of characters

exercises.title: ft_strstr
requirements: Submit ft_strstr.c in ex6/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: char *ft_strstr(char *str, char *to_find);
Reproduce strstr behavior as specified by its manual page.
exercises.goal: Search for a sequence and return the location of its first occurrence without allocating or copying it.
exercises.connection: Reuse pairwise character comparison at several candidate offsets in one source string.
exercises.observe: Show failed candidate positions before a match, then a returned pointer into the original string. Include the empty-needle result pointing to the original start and a no-match NULL result.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Find a substring and return its address

exercises.title: ft_atoi
requirements: Submit ft_atoi.c in ex7/.
Authorized functions: none.
Prototype: int ft_atoi(char *str);
Convert the initial numeric portion of the string to an integer.
Skip any initial whitespace recognized by isspace(3).
Accept any sequence of '+' and '-' signs; an odd number of '-' signs makes the result negative.
Read digits until the first non-digit, then return the value accumulated so far.
Overflow and underflow handling are not required; results may be undefined in those cases.
exercises.goal: Build an integer from text while keeping whitespace, signs, and digits as distinct parsing stages.
exercises.connection: Combine character classification, string scanning, and arithmetic. This exercise accepts multiple signs, unlike many ordinary atoi descriptions.
exercises.observe: Use ASCII input '  --+42x7': show skipped spaces, sign flipping twice back to positive, accumulation 0→4→42, and stopping at x so the later 7 is ignored. Show no-digit input returning zero.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Parse whitespace, signs, and decimal digits

title: C System Interface: Program Arguments
summary: Receive arguments in main through argc and argv. Print the program name, visit the supplied argument strings in different orders, and sort them by character codes.
why: Command-line arguments let one compiled program work with different inputs. argv connects shell input with arrays, strings, and multiple levels of pointers.

statedGoals.text: Develop programs using system arguments and command-line interfaces, manipulating program parameters dynamically.

interpretation: The numbered exercises specifically teach argc and argv rather than file descriptors or broader system calls. Learn which slot is the program name, where user arguments begin, how bounds are derived from argc, and how pointer swapping can reorder text without rewriting it.

exercises.title: ft_print_program_name
requirements: Submit ft_print_program_name.c in ex0/.
Authorized functions: write.
This is a complete program, so include main.
Print the program's own name followed by a newline.
exercises.goal: Understand how main receives the invocation name as the first argument string.
exercises.connection: The shell starts the compiled program; main receives a pointer array whose entries point to strings like those studied earlier.
exercises.observe: Show './demo red' becoming argc=2 and argv entries './demo', 'red', NULL. Follow argv[0] to its characters and output only './demo\n'.

exercises.title: ft_print_params
requirements: Submit ft_print_params.c in ex1/.
Authorized functions: write.
This is a complete program, so include main.
Print all given arguments except argv[0], one per line, in command-line order.
exercises.goal: Traverse the argument array and, for each pointer, traverse the referenced string.
exercises.connection: Nest string printing inside an array traversal, starting at index 1 rather than 0.
exercises.observe: Highlight the argv slot and each character independently. Show argv[0] excluded, each newline appended, and no user arguments producing no output.

exercises.title: ft_rev_params
requirements: Submit ft_rev_params.c in ex2/.
Authorized functions: write.
This is a complete program, so include main.
Print all given arguments except argv[0], one per line, in reverse command-line order.
exercises.goal: Visit argument slots backward while printing the characters within each string forward.
exercises.connection: Change only the array traversal direction from ft_print_params; the string-output operation stays the same.
exercises.observe: For './demo red blue', show the index moving 2→1 and output 'blue\nred\n'. The letters inside each argument are not reversed and the argv contents do not change.

exercises.title: ft_sort_params
requirements: Submit ft_sort_params.c in ex3/.
Authorized functions: write.
This is a complete program, so include main.
Print all given arguments except argv[0], sorted in ASCII order, one argument per line.
exercises.goal: Combine text comparison with array sorting while preserving each argument's characters.
exercises.connection: Use strcmp-like logic to decide order and the pointer module's swap pattern to exchange argv entries.
exercises.observe: Show pointers for 'blue', 'Red', and 'apple' changing slots while their character buffers stay in place. Highlight that uppercase R precedes lowercase a in ASCII order; exclude argv[0] from sorting and output.

title: C-Function-Pointers
summary: Give a function to another function so that the same loop can perform different actions, transform values, test conditions, or compare elements.
why: Separating the traversal from the action lets you reuse one algorithm with several behaviors. It also teaches the difference between data addresses and callable function addresses.
prerequisites: malloc for a new result array

statedGoals.text: Use function pointers to process arrays and evaluate sorting; the cover also mentions a basic calculator.

interpretation: The actual exercises develop callbacks: apply an action, collect returned values, evaluate a predicate, count matches, and check order through a comparison function. A callback parameter receives a copied function address, and f(tab[i]) passes an integer value rather than the address of the array element.

sourceNotes.text: The summary mentions a basic calculator, but the contents and complete exercise pages contain only ex0 through ex4. No calculator exercise is present; do not invent an assignment.
General submission rules require cc with -Wall -Wextra -Werror, the Norm, only requested files, and a main only when a program is requested.

exercises.title: ft_foreach
requirements: Submit ex0/ft_foreach.c; authorized functions: None.
Prototype: void ft_foreach(int *tab, int length, void(*f)(int));
Apply f to every integer element in array order.
The example passes &ft_putnbr as the callback to display the integers.
exercises.goal: Understand that the loop chooses which element to visit while f chooses what to do with that element's copied value.
exercises.connection: You already passed data to functions. Now pass the address of a function and call it during the traversal.

title: C-Structures
summary: Group related values in a struct, access its members directly or through a pointer, and build an allocated array of records from strings.
why: Real programs need to keep different kinds of information together. Structures let you describe a record once and create many independent records with that shape.

statedGoals.text: Use fundamental C structures and memory management to store and manipulate data.
Move from simple types to arrays and then structures.
Use structures to group members of different types, define the type first, and then create variables of that type.

interpretation: The module connects the layout of arrays with compound records, then combines borrowed string pointers, owned string copies, dynamic allocation, sentinel termination, and output. A type definition describes a shape; a variable declaration creates an object of that shape.

sourceNotes.text: The tutorial's automatic array without an initializer has indeterminate values. Do not execute the later example that reads an uninitialized element; teach initialization before reads. Static-duration objects have different initialization rules.

exercises.observe: Show the type declaration as a shape without runtime storage. Once variables are declared, show separate learner objects and highlight only the member changed. Connect ptr->age to the same member as (*ptr).age without pretending every member is tightly packed with no padding.

title: C-Preprocessor
summary: Use headers to share declarations and definitions, and use macros to name constants and expressions before compilation.
why: A project with several files needs shared descriptions of its functions and types. The preprocessor prepares the text that the compiler will read.

statedGoals.text: Explore headers, macros, and conditional directives to improve code modularity and readability.

interpretation: The exercises introduce a shared function interface, a named boolean interface, and an expression macro. Include guards and parenthesized macro expressions are useful teaching connections to conditional preprocessing and safe textual substitution, even though the exercise paragraphs do not separately prescribe an include-guard design.

sourceNotes.text: The supplied main only includes ft_boolean.h but calls write, so the teaching header should include the declaration needed for write. The header's authorized-functions field is None; this does not mean the supplied main is prohibited from its printed write call.

The two displayed shell examples both show ./a.out but describe the alternative even/odd argument-count messages. Explain actual argc - 1 parity rather than implying identical invocations give different results.

ABS is an expression macro, not a runtime function call. A demonstration should use a safe pure value such as -7; minimum signed-int negation and arguments with side effects require separate caveats and are not specified assignment cases.

exercises.title: ft.h
requirements: Submit ex0/ft.h; authorized functions: None.
Include these prototypes: void ft_putchar(char c); void ft_swap(int *a, int *b); void ft_putstr(char *str); int ft_strlen(char *str); int ft_strcmp(char *s1, char *s2).
exercises.goal: Understand how a declaration tells another source file which function name, return type, and parameters it may use.
exercises.connection: Reuse familiar output, swap, length, and comparison functions, now separating their declarations from their implementations.
exercises.observe: Show #include expanding the header into source before compilation. Mark prototypes as declarations with no runtime variable mutation or function body execution. Explain that implementations are still needed when the program is linked.

exercises.title: ft_boolean.h

exercises.connection: Combine the header interface from ex0 with earlier modulo arithmetic and if statements. argc includes the executable name, so argc - 1 counts user arguments.
exercises.observe: Separate preprocessing from runtime steps. Expand EVEN(argc - 1), show the actual user-argument count and its remainder on division by two, then highlight the selected branch and matching terminal message.

exercises.title: ft_abs.h

exercises.connection: Reuse comparison, unary minus, and the conditional operator introduced by the boolean example.
exercises.observe: Show ABS(-7) expand into a parenthesized conditional expression, then evaluate the condition and selected value. No callback parameter or call frame is created by the macro itself. Use pure arguments so repeated substitution does not hide side effects.

title: C-Libft
summary: Package familiar C functions into a static library, first with a shell script and then with a Makefile that rebuilds only what needs rebuilding.
why: A library makes your functions reusable across programs. Separate compilation and dependency rules avoid repeating the same manual compilation work.

statedGoals.text: Create libft.a as a static C library and automate its compilation with a Makefile.
Create a first Makefile, understand its syntax, and explore the features needed for the present build goals.
Use separate compilation so source files that have not changed need not be compiled again.

interpretation: The module joins file organization with the build lifecycle: .c source becomes .o object code, object files are collected in an archive, and a program can link against that archive. Make determines needed work using targets, prerequisites, and file timestamps.

sourceNotes.text: Exercise 1 unusually requires a root main.c to be compiled and its main.o included in libft.a. Preserve this source-specific requirement rather than silently replacing it with usual library conventions.

The tutorial says to add fclean, but its next verification sentence says make clean should clean everything. The defined clean/fclean distinction and exercise 1 rules make clear that fclean is the full cleanup.
Only the Makefile is submitted for ex1; the evaluator supplies the source files and header. Avoid treating the supplied files as extra student submission files.

exercises.title: Tutorial
requirements: Tutorial practice, not a numbered submission exercise; continues through PDF page 11.
Make a working directory containing ft_strdup.c and a main.c test; verify manual compilation before writing the Makefile.
Create a file named exactly Makefile with variables NAME = test_strdup, SOURCES = ft_strdup.c main.c, and OBJECTS = $(SOURCES:.c=.o).
Add a target depending on the object files and link them with cc; observe implicit .c-to-.o rules, run the executable, and inspect generated files.
Add clean to remove objects and fclean to remove objects and the program; add CFLAGS += -Wall and observe the flag during compilation.
Create a ft_range subdirectory with ft_range.c and a main.c; extend the Makefile to build and clean both test programs.
Delete one object file and run make all; run make all again without changes and investigate dependencies and timestamps.
exercises.goal: Understand why make compiles a missing or outdated object but can leave an up-to-date object alone.
exercises.connection: Turn the manual cc commands learned earlier into dependency rules over familiar source files.
exercises.observe: Show the source, object, and executable files with their dependency connections and timestamps. Highlight each actual command, then compare first build, unchanged second build, one-source rebuild, clean, and fclean. Makefile recipe lines require a real tab.

title: C-File-Operations
summary: Use file descriptors and system calls to read files in chunks and reproduce selected behaviors of display_file, cat, tail, and hexdump.
why: Files may be larger than a program's buffer. Correct file handling tracks how many bytes were read or written, handles errors, and closes resources.
prerequisites: malloc and free for later exercises

statedGoals.text: Reproduce common file operations, including reading, writing, and manipulating files through system calls.
Read the manuals for every authorized function in the cat exercise.

interpretation: The progression moves from displaying one file to concatenating input streams, keeping only the last requested bytes, and formatting bytes as hexadecimal and readable characters. The lessons should distinguish file storage, the program's buffer, descriptor/offset state, stdout, and stderr.

sourceNotes.text: The display_file paragraph says all file arguments are valid but also explicitly requires a Cannot read file. error. Preserve the failure behavior in the analysis and teaching demonstration.
The cat fixed-array limit is described as a little less than 30 ko, not an exact byte number. Do not silently turn it into an exact boundary.

hexdump is requested without redirection. The assignment only singles out -C; detailed system-command formatting should be checked against the relevant manual/system behavior before implementing a full replica.

requirements: Submit ex0/Makefile and program files; authorized functions: close, open, read, write.
Create the ft_display_file program that writes only the named file's contents to standard output.
Provide Makefile targets all, clean, and fclean; name the binary ft_display_file.
malloc is forbidden; use a fixed-size array.

Write error messages to their reserved error output, each with a newline: File name missing. when no filename is supplied; Too many arguments. when more than one is supplied; Cannot read file. when the file cannot be read.
exercises.goal: Move file bytes through a small reusable buffer into terminal output while checking arguments and I/O results.
exercises.connection: Extend write-based output by obtaining the bytes from a file rather than a string already in memory. Reuse loops and copied pointer addresses for buffers.
exercises.observe: Show open producing a descriptor, each read filling the buffer and advancing the file position, write transferring exactly the valid byte count, EOF returning 0, and close ending access. Explain that buffer bytes need not be a null-terminated string. Include a compact error branch and avoid outputting stale buffer contents.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Read a file through a fixed buffer

exercises.observe: Trace a small input such as ABCDEFG with -c 3, showing each incoming byte and how retained bytes change until EFG is printed. Show the selected teaching algorithm plainly and distinguish byte count from character or line count.

exercises.title: hexdump

title: C-Linked-Lists
summary: Build a chain of nodes, then create, inspect, change, reverse, and sort that chain.
why: A linked list can grow without requiring its nodes to sit next to each other in memory. Correct links and ownership keep every node reachable and allow memory to be released safely.

statedGoals.text: Implement functions for creating, modifying, and manipulating singly linked lists, including insertion, deletion, and sorting.
Build programming foundations through practice, reasoning, and peer learning.

interpretation: The exercises progress from allocating one node to maintaining a whole chain. They develop the distinction between a node, its payload, its next pointer, and the caller's head pointer; later exercises combine ownership with callback-driven algorithms.

From ex1 onward, the evaluator uses its own ft_create_elem; arrange a suitable declaration.
Compile with cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror, follow the Norm, and submit only the requested files.

exercises.title: ft_list_push_strs
requirements: Submit ft_list_push_strs.c and ft_list.h; ft_create_elem is authorized.
Create a list containing the strings pointed to by the elements of strs; size is the number of strs entries.

exercises.title: ft_list_clear
requirements: Submit ft_list_clear.c and ft_list.h; free is authorized.
Remove and free every link; use free_fct to free each data payload.

exercises.title: ft_list_at
requirements: Submit ft_list_at.c and ft_list.h; no functions are authorized.
