title: C-Binary-Trees
summary: Create nodes with left and right child links, traverse them in different orders, and build a searchable ordered tree.
why: Trees represent branching relationships. Their traversals show how the same stored values produce different visit orders, and sorted insertion makes comparison guide a search.

statedGoals.text: Implement and manipulate binary trees in C.
Build programming foundations through practice, reasoning, and peer learning.

interpretation: The progression teaches safe recursive exploration of branching structures, callback placement, search-tree ordering, and the difference between visiting by depth and visiting by level.
commonRequirements: Use t_btree containing struct s_btree *left, struct s_btree *right, and void *item, defined in ft_btree.h (PDF page 9).
Submit ft_btree.h for each exercise; from ex1 onward the evaluator uses its own btree_create_node.
Compile with cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror, follow the Norm, and submit only requested files.

exercises.title: btree_create_node
requirements: Submit btree_create_node.c and ft_btree.h; malloc is authorized.
Allocate a new node, set item to the supplied argument, set other fields to 0, and return its address.
Prototype: t_btree *btree_create_node(void *item);
exercises.goal: Create a tree node whose payload refers to an existing object and whose children are initially absent.
exercises.connection: Extends list-node creation from one next link to two child links.
exercises.observe: A node allocation appears, item holds a copied address, and both left and right are NULL.

exercises.title: btree_apply_prefix
requirements: Submit btree_apply_prefix.c and ft_btree.h; no functions are authorized.
Apply the given function to every node item using prefix traversal.
Prototype: void btree_apply_prefix(t_btree *root, void (*applyf)(void *));
exercises.goal: Visit the current node before its left and right subtrees.
exercises.connection: Combines callback traversal with recursive function calls.
exercises.observe: The visit happens before descending. Show the call stack, NULL base cases, and root-left-right output order.

exercises.title: btree_apply_infix
requirements: Submit btree_apply_infix.c and ft_btree.h; no functions are authorized.
Apply the given function to every node item using infix traversal.
Prototype: void btree_apply_infix(t_btree *root, void (*applyf)(void *));
exercises.goal: Visit the left subtree, then the current node, then the right subtree.
exercises.connection: Changes only where the callback occurs relative to prefix recursion; in an ordered tree it reveals ascending values.
exercises.observe: A call must finish the left subtree before visiting its own node. Highlight left-root-right output.

exercises.title: btree_apply_suffix
requirements: Submit btree_apply_suffix.c and ft_btree.h; no functions are authorized.
Apply the given function to every node item using suffix traversal.
Prototype: void btree_apply_suffix(t_btree *root, void (*applyf)(void *));
exercises.goal: Finish both child subtrees before visiting their parent.
exercises.connection: Completes the traversal-order comparison; children-first order is useful when a later cleanup operation depends on child completion.
exercises.observe: The parent visit waits until both recursive calls return. Highlight left-right-root output.

exercises.title: btree_insert_data
requirements: Submit btree_insert_data.c and ft_btree.h; btree_create_node is authorized.
Insert item in a sorted tree using a strcmp-like comparison function; values lower than a node go left and higher or equal values go right.
The root parameter points to the root pointer; on the first call it should point to NULL.
Prototype: void btree_insert_data(t_btree **root, void *item, int (*cmpf)(void *, void *));
exercises.goal: Let comparisons select a branch until an empty child slot is found, then update that slot through its address.
exercises.connection: Generalizes sorted-list insertion to a two-way branching structure.
exercises.observe: Track each comparison and chosen link. Equality goes right. The new node changes one previously NULL link, including root for an empty tree.

exercises.title: btree_search_item
requirements: Submit btree_search_item.c and ft_btree.h; no functions are authorized.
Return the first item matching data_ref under cmpf, traversing in infix order; return NULL if no matching element is found.
Prototype: void *btree_search_item(t_btree *root, void *data_ref, int (*cmpf)(void *, void *));
exercises.goal: Carry a matching payload address back through recursive calls and stop once the required first match is found.
exercises.connection: Uses infix traversal and comparator callbacks; unlike insertion, the requirement explicitly selects a traversal order.
exercises.observe: Visits occur in infix order. The result is the stored item address, not a newly copied payload or the containing tree-node address.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Search a tree in infix order

exercises.title: btree_level_count
requirements: Submit btree_level_count.c and ft_btree.h; no functions are authorized.
Return the size of the tree's largest branch.
Prototype: int btree_level_count(t_btree *root);
The PDF does not explicitly define an empty-tree result or whether branch size counts nodes or edges.
exercises.goal: Compare the heights returned by the two child branches and extend the longer one by the current node.
exercises.connection: Applies recursive return values and maximum selection to branching data.
exercises.observe: Show each child's returned height before the parent combines them. Label the representative simulation's convention: NULL = 0 levels, leaf = 1 level.

exercises.title: btree_apply_by_level
requirements: Submit btree_apply_by_level.c and ft_btree.h; malloc and free are authorized.
Visit the tree level by level and call applyf for every node.
Pass item, current_level (root 0, children 1, grandchildren 2, etc.), and is_first_elem (1 for the first node at that level, otherwise 0).
Prototype: void btree_apply_by_level(t_btree *root, void (*applyf)(void *item, int current_level, int is_first_elem));
exercises.goal: Keep shallower nodes ahead of deeper ones and identify the start of each level.
exercises.connection: Uses dynamic structures to manage work; contrasts with the recursive depth-first traversals.
exercises.observe: Show the pending queue, level number, and first-element flag as nodes are visited. A queue is a representative technique, not a mandated algorithm.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Visit a tree level by level

ambiguities: btree_level_count says largest branch size without defining nodes versus edges or the NULL result; state the simulation convention.
Within-level left-to-right order in ex7 is conventional but is not explicitly specified in this PDF.

title: Square
summary: Draw a rectangle using coordinates, loops, and border rules. Five variants share the same logic but use different corner and edge characters.
why: This project turns a visual specification into precise cases, tests narrow rectangles, and connects small functions across source files.

statedGoals.text: Create a program that prints rectangles with varying patterns using supplied dimensions.
Every team member must understand the complete project and explain the work at defense.

interpretation: The central learning task is to translate row and column positions into character choices, place overlapping corner cases in a safe order, and test a reusable drawing function independently of main.
commonRequirements: Only one Rush 0X variant is required: choose a team member's first name, convert its first letter to A=1 through Z=26, and use that value modulo 5 (PDF page 4).
Team size is 2, 3, or 4. Every team member must understand the complete program.
Follow the Norm and compile with cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror. Handle errors coherently, with an error message or by returning control.
No bonus section is present in this PDF.

exercises.title: Rush0X
requirements: Submit ex00/main.c, ft_putchar.c, and rush0X.c for the assigned variant; write is the only authorized function.
The three files compile together; ft_putchar.c contains ft_putchar, and rush0X.c contains rush(int x, int y).
rush must print a rectangle x characters wide and y lines high.
The function must never crash or loop indefinitely. Defense replaces main to test other dimensions, including the shown rush(123, 42).
Handle invalid dimensions coherently; the PDF permits printing an error or simply returning control.
exercises.goal: Separate rectangle traversal, character selection, and output so changing the dimensions does not require changing the program logic.
exercises.connection: Combines conditions, loops, and parameter passing into a small multi-file project.
exercises.observe: Watch row and column counters, the chosen output character, and terminal growth. Width 1 or height 1 makes corner conditions overlap.
exercises.suggestedSimulation: Draw a rectangle one character at a time

exercises.title: Rush 00
requirements: Apply the shared Rush0X requirements when this is the assigned variant; it is not an additional required project.
Use o for corners, - for horizontal edges, | for vertical edges, and spaces inside.
Examples: (5,3) prints o---o, |   |, o---o on separate lines; (5,1) prints o---o; (1,1) prints o; (1,5) prints o, |, |, |, o on separate lines.
The additional (4,4) example appears on PDF page 13.
exercises.goal: Identify corners before edges so narrow rectangles remain correct.
exercises.connection: Applies the common coordinate-based drawing loop to one border pattern.
exercises.observe: Highlight which border rule selected o, -, |, or a space, and show a newline after each row.

exercises.title: Rush 01
requirements: Apply the shared Rush0X requirements when this is the assigned variant.
Top-left /, top-right backslash, bottom-left backslash, bottom-right /; all noncorner edge characters are * and the interior is spaces.
Examples: (5,1) uses the top edge; (1,1) prints /; (1,5) prints /, *, *, *, backslash on separate lines.
The additional (4,4) example appears on PDF page 15.
exercises.goal: Distinguish all four corners and represent a backslash correctly in a C character literal.
exercises.connection: Adds direction-specific corners to the common rectangle loop.
exercises.observe: Show how one coordinate chooses a corner, and how the top or left rule takes priority when dimensions collapse to one.

exercises.title: Rush 02
requirements: Apply the shared Rush0X requirements when this is the assigned variant.
Both top corners are A, both bottom corners C, all other edge characters B, and the interior is spaces.
Examples: (5,3) prints ABBBA, B   B, CBBBC; (5,1) prints ABBBA; (1,1) prints A; (1,5) prints A, B, B, B, C on separate lines.
The additional (4,4) example appears on PDF page 17.
exercises.goal: Use the current row to distinguish top corners from bottom corners.
exercises.connection: Reuses the common rectangle traversal with different character decisions.
exercises.observe: The same column position prints A at the top, B on a vertical side, and C at the bottom.

exercises.title: Rush 03
requirements: Apply the shared Rush0X requirements when this is the assigned variant.
Both left corners are A, both right corners C, all other edge characters B, and the interior is spaces.
Examples: (5,3) prints ABBBC, B   B, ABBBC; (5,1) prints ABBBC; (1,1) prints A; (1,5) prints A, B, B, B, A on separate lines.
The additional (4,4) example appears on PDF page 19.
exercises.goal: Use the current column to distinguish left corners from right corners.
exercises.connection: Contrasts with Rush 02: changing row-based corner decisions to column-based ones changes the pattern.
exercises.observe: Top and bottom rows share a pattern. At width 1 the left corner wins, so both end characters are A.

exercises.title: Rush 04
requirements: Apply the shared Rush0X requirements when this is the assigned variant.
Top-left and bottom-right corners are A; top-right and bottom-left are C; other edges are B; interior is spaces.
Examples: (5,3) prints ABBBC, B   B, CBBBA; (5,1) prints ABBBC; (1,1) prints A; (1,5) prints A, B, B, B, C on separate lines.
The additional (4,4) example appears on PDF page 21.
exercises.goal: Combine row and column checks to distinguish diagonally opposed corner pairs.
exercises.connection: Brings together the corner decisions explored in the other variants.
exercises.observe: Highlight the active row and column together; compare the normal rectangle to width 1, height 1, and 1 by 1.

The PDF does not demand a specific message or behavior for nonpositive dimensions beyond coherent error handling and no crash or infinite loop.

title: Sky_Scraper
summary: Solve a 4 by 4 height puzzle: each row and column contains heights 1 to 4 once, and clues specify how many boxes are visible from each edge.
why: The puzzle connects validation, arrays, conditions, and a search that can undo an unsuccessful choice. Visibility counting gives a concrete rule for testing a candidate solution.

statedGoals.text: Develop a program that solves a 4x4 visibility puzzle by arranging box heights according to input constraints.
Every team member must understand the full project and explain its details at defense.

interpretation: The requirements suggest decomposing the program into parsing, row/column uniqueness checks, directional visibility counts, a search strategy, and output. Backtracking is a representative technique; the PDF requires a valid first solution, not one particular algorithm.
commonRequirements: Team project; all teammates must understand the work and attend defense.
Follow the Norm and compile with cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o rush-01 *.c.
No bonus section or larger-grid requirement appears in this PDF.

exercises.title: Rush-01
requirements: Submit all necessary files in ex00/; authorized functions are write, malloc, and free.
Fill a 4x4 grid with heights 1 through 4, placing each height exactly once in every row and column.
Each row must satisfy visibility clues from left and right; each column must satisfy clues from up and down. A taller box hides smaller boxes behind it.
Print the first solution encountered.

Accept the demonstrated single argument containing sixteen characters from '1' to '4', separated by spaces, ordered: four column-up, four column-down, four row-left, four row-right clues. Other input is an error (PDF page 10).
Print Error followed by a newline for invalid input or when no solution exists.
For the example clues 4 3 2 1 1 2 2 2 4 3 2 1 1 2 2 2, the shown rows are 1 2 3 4; 2 3 4 1; 3 4 1 2; 4 1 2 3, with spaces between values and a newline after each row.
exercises.goal: Turn clues into checks, try one height at a time, and undo a choice when it cannot lead to a valid solution.
exercises.connection: Builds on rectangle coordinates, arrays, parsing, and recursion. Unlike simple calculation, a failed partial state requires returning to an earlier decision.
exercises.observe: First trace argument positions into clue slots. Then highlight a candidate grid cell, duplicate checks, maximum-so-far visibility counts, recursive descent, rejection, and resetting a cell to empty. Clearly label partial versus complete line checks.

ambiguities: The PDF specifies the demonstrated input form as the only acceptable form; it does not separately enumerate every malformed whitespace case.
Backtracking is an instructional interpretation, not an explicitly required implementation.
There is no larger-grid bonus in this supplied version.

title: Rosetta_Stone
summary: Read a configurable number dictionary and convert a decimal number into words, including numbers larger than an unsigned int.
why: This combines parsing, file operations, dynamic memory, and decomposition of a large task into reusable steps. The output must follow dictionary contents rather than hard-coded language strings.

statedGoals.text: Create a program that converts numbers to written words with a dictionary of customizable value mappings.
Every team member must understand the full project and explain the work at defense.

interpretation: The project trains a data-driven design: keep large numbers as text, parse and validate dictionary entries, decompose numeric text into supported components, resolve their words, and clean up both on success and failure.
commonRequirements: Team project; all teammates must understand the work and attend defense.
Follow the Norm and compile with cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror.
The Makefile must provide the executable target NAME, clean, and fclean; evaluation runs make fclean then make.
No bonus section is present in this PDF.

exercises.title: rush-02
requirements: Submit Makefile and all necessary files under ex00/; name the executable rush-02. Authorized functions: write, malloc, free, open, read, close.
Accept one argument for the number using the reference dictionary, or two arguments with a replacement dictionary path first and the number second.
Invalid numeric input prints Error followed by a newline. Support values beyond unsigned int; the example explicitly accepts 0 despite the prose saying positive number.
Parse the supplied reference dictionary and use its stored values for output; values can be changed.
Dictionary entries have number, zero or more spaces, colon, zero or more spaces, and printable text. Handle dictionary numbers like atoi and trim spaces before/after the value (PDF page 9).
Reference keys remain present, values can change, extra entries may be added, entry order is arbitrary, and empty lines can occur.
Use the original entries when decomposing numbers; an extra key 54 does not replace combining the original keys 50 and 4.
Print Dict Error followed by a newline if dictionary parsing fails or the dictionary cannot resolve the requested value.
Free every heap allocation correctly; this is checked in evaluation.
Examples: 42 produces forty two; 0 produces zero; 10.4 produces Error; 100000 produces one hundred thousand. If key 20 is changed to hey everybody !, output those dictionary words for 20.
exercises.goal: Separate reading and parsing data from converting a number, and avoid overflowing an integer by processing its digits as text.
exercises.connection: Combines string handling, dynamic storage, file reads, structures, and build rules into a complete program.
exercises.observe: Show file bytes entering a buffer, a parsed key/value entry, digit groups and selected dictionary keys, accumulated terminal words, and cleanup. Contrast invalid number Error with dictionary Dict Error.

ambiguities: The prose says positive number, but the explicit example accepts 0; the teaching material should use nonnegative decimal input and note that example.
Dictionary keys are parsed like atoi while the command-line number rejects 10.4; these are distinct parsing contexts.
The reference dictionary's complete contents are not attached within this PDF, so its full key set cannot be reconstructed from this document alone.
Behavior for duplicate dictionary keys and exact output spacing outside the examples is not separately specified.
